transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: 1h24m
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Michael (Cobalt CTO), Aisha (Lead ML Eng), Daniel (Platform Eng)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll try to keep this hands-on. Today's workshop is focused on throughput tuning — continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs and token limits — and practical steps for a pilot on your on-prem cluster. quick intro?

[00:18] Michael: yeah thanks. I'm Michael, CTO at Cobalt. We've got a production inference fleet (mostly on prem for PHI reasons), running a mix of 4x A100s and a few older 3090-ish hosts. latency targets: 95th under 400ms, 99th under 800ms for chat cases. cost is a big constraint.

[00:34] Aisha: hi everyone. I'm Aisha, lead ml eng. Our main workload is triage chat + extraction. messages are typically 30-120 tokens; system prompts add another 50 tokens. we saw big tail latency at peak and cold-KV misses.

[00:49] Daniel: Daniel, infra. We run on locked-down VPC/on-prem network, strict egress rules, KMS via internal HSM. happy to share access but need to keep it air-gapped.

[01:05] Samir: perfect, that's exactly the constraints we want to tune around. quick agenda: 1) explain how continuous batching and the scheduler interact, 2) go over key knobs (max_num_seqs, token caps, slot sizing, prefetch/kvcache warmup), 3) tradeoffs vs quantization and on-prem HW, 4) recommended configs and pilot plan.

[01:26] Lena: short caveat — some transcription artifacts, I'll drop links in the follow-up: benchmark sheet, sample scripts, and a kv-warmup helper.

[01:34] Samir: ok starting with the scheduler model. At a high level Redwood's scheduler groups requests by model and compatibility, does continuous batching to pack seqs onto GPU until max_num_seqs is reached or a latency window expires. The knobs control both batch packing and fairness.

[01:56] Michael: can you explain "max_num_seqs" in plain terms again — we keep hearing it but unclear real-world effect.

[02:05] Lena: yeah so max_num_seqs is the maximum number of sequences (requests) the runtime will pack into a multi-sequence batch for a single attention pass. higher max_num_seqs increases throughput but can raise tail latency due to head-of-line waiting — esp when you have peaky arrival patterns. think of it as the max packing width for the GPU kernel.

[02:28] Aisha: so with our mix of short prompts and some long ones, would a higher max_num_seqs help?

[02:33] Lena: it depends. If the request length distribution is skewed short, raising max_num_seqs gives big throughput wins because you amortize attention ops. But if you have even a few long sequences, they can increase GPU memory pressure and cause eviction of KV entries. Also long sequences cause other sequences in the batch to wait until the bigger seq finishes decoding steps.

[02:56] Daniel: we saw memory OOMs in the past when we cranked batch width. is that expected?

[03:01] Lena: yes — GPU memory scales roughly with (max_num_seqs * max_seq_length * hidden_size) for kv cache in many models. We usually recommend starting with conservative max_num_seqs (like 8-16) on A100s for 2k-ish kv profiles then iteratively increase. For your A100s we can target 16 as a starting point.

[03:22] Samir: one helpful pattern is adaptive capacity: start the scheduler with a lower max_num_seqs under load spikes and let the autoscaler add slots. Redwood's Dedicated also supports capacity tiers so you can reserve headroom for spikes without impacting tail latency.

[03:40] Michael: curious — how do you trade off continuous batching versus strict immediate scheduling for low-latency calls (like anticipation tasks)?

[03:47] Lena: that's the classic latency vs cost tradeoff. We have per-route latency SLOs where you set a tight latency window and the scheduler will prioritize immediate batching (smaller tolerances) for those requests, falling back to reserved low-latency slots. For cheaper routes, you can increase batching window to get more token throughput.

[04:06] Aisha: what about token limits? we currently enforce a 1024 token max per request. Is that causing additional batching inefficiency?

[04:12] Lena: token ceilings affect the sample-length distribution. If you frequently truncate or chunk, you may be increasing the number of requests and the effective per-user token tax. Two knobs: reduce per-request token ceiling when you want to cap compute, or move to partial-response streaming so you avoid blocking large token counts in a single batch.

[04:36] Daniel: you mentioned kv warmup earlier — we see cold-kv hits kill throughput. What's the best practice for on-prem?

[04:44] Lena: warmup is critical. We recommend a multi-step approach: 1) persistent KV pre-seeding for frequently used prompts (small footprint), 2) burst prefetch for scheduled heavy windows (spawn async requests early), and 3) background async prewarm tasks triggered by trace-based heuristics. For air-gapped on-prem, it's just scripts that run locally and populate the runtime's KV store.

[05:09] Samir: practical tip — at the start of business-hours run a prewarm that mirrors top X prompts (we usually pick top 500-1k), at lower cost than cold misses. We have a kv-warmup helper script I'll share.

[05:20] Michael: does warmup add undue extra costs? we bill by token / cycles.

[05:25] Samir: some cost, yes — but it's far cheaper than paying for tail latency remediation or double-generation retries. In our experience warmup reduces overall token spend by avoiding repeated recomputation.

[05:36] Aisha: how about eviction policies? we need to control per-customer KV quota because mem pressure occasionally spikes.

[05:42] Lena: set per-tenant kv_capacity, and an eviction policy like LRU with bias for recent conversational contexts. You can also set a hotset whitelist for critical prompt templates that never evict. For strict memory caps, use per-customer shard weights so one noisy tenant doesn't evict another's entries.

[06:02] Daniel: our infra requires strict resource isolation. How does Redwood Dedicated handle multi-tenant vs per-customer pools?

[06:09] Samir: Dedicated supports GPU pools per-customer with shard weights and hard token quotas. You can run single-tenant pools for HIPAA workloads. For mixed tenancy we provide soft and hard quotas with automated fallback to smaller quantized models for overflow.

[06:24] Michael: speaking of quantization, can int4/8 help us here? we want cost savings but worry about quality regressions.

[06:31] Lena: quantization can lower memory for kv cache and model weights. int8 is typically safe for many open models; int4 is higher risk but often acceptable for purely classification or reranking tasks. For chat and extraction you need to run a small eval set — we can help with that. Also quantized kernels change performance curves: lower memory per seq means you can increase max_num_seqs but watch for numerical degeneration in generation.

[06:58] Aisha: can you share a quick example config?

[07:02] Lena: sure — conceptual example: 
- route: /chat-lowlatency -> max_num_seqs: 4, latency_window_ms: 25, reserved_slots: 2
- route: /chat-batch -> max_num_seqs: 24, latency_window_ms: 120, prefetch: true, kv_prefetch_list: top_1k_prompts
(we'll attach exact helm values)

[07:28] Daniel: when you say latency_window_ms, is that the time scheduler waits to fill batch?

[07:33] Lena: yes it's the max time the scheduler will hold an open batch before dispatching even if it's not full. Lower window favors latency, higher favors throughput.

[07:41] Michael: any heuristics for selecting that?

[07:44] Samir: start by measuring inter-arrival time distribution for the route. If median inter-arrival is 10ms, a 50ms window will likely collect ~5 requests. We usually pick a window that's a small multiple of median inter-arrival to balance.

[07:58] Aisha: we also have bursts from nightly jobs that open many sessions. Do you recommend smoothing them at router level?

[08:05] Lena: yes. Use client-side rate limiting + server-side priority windows. Redwood supports priority windows where internal background jobs get lower priority slots and are throttled when user-facing SLOs are active.

[08:19] Samir: demo time — Lena, can you pull up the live scheduler dashboard and show metrics?

[08:24] Lena: sure, sharing screen.

[08:30] [08:30] (screen share noise)

[08:35] Lena: here's an example timeline: request in, scheduler assigns slot, batches accumulate, prefetch kicks in, GPU kernel executes, kv cache hit rate is recorded. Notice the correlation between kv hit-rate and 99th percentile latency — when hit-rate drops from 92% to 60% tail jumps.

[08:58] Michael: do you track per-model kernel choice? we've compiled a few custom ops that perform better.

[09:04] Lena: runtime picks kernels based on model arch and seq length. We have a kernel selector that prefers fused-attention kernels for medium seq lengths. If you have custom kernels we can register them but need to validate correctness; we can do that in pilot.

[09:19] Daniel: what about cold starts after code deploys? we saw a 10x latency spike for 15 minutes after rolling.

[09:26] Lena: rolling upgrades should include a staged prewarm: first bring up one instance, run kv and model warm calls, then route traffic. We also have a graceful rebalancer that moves hot shards slowly rather than all at once.

[09:40] Aisha: how does continuous batching interact with streaming responses? for us streaming is important — we show partial answers as they come.

[09:48] Lena: streaming complicates batching because you need to interleave generation steps and flush partial tokens. The scheduler supports streaming-aware batching where the runtime can emit early tokens per-sequence while continuing to pack further sequences; but that reduces packing efficiency. There's a middle ground: chunked streaming where you only stream after the first few tokens to collect better packing.

[10:11] Samir: question from my side — have you considered fallbacks to smaller quantized models for peaks?

[10:16] Michael: yes we've toyed with it but worry about quality.

[10:19] Lena: a/B fallback is the right pattern: keep a light-weight model for initial replies and then re-rank or refine on a heavier model when capacity allows. That reduces tail pressure and is faster for many intent-detection tasks.

[10:31] Daniel: about prefetching — you recommended an async prefetch; how do we avoid overfilling KV with stale entries?

[10:38] Lena: use TTLs and access-based TTL refresh. Prefetch only top-N heuristics and use an LRU eviction that respects per-customer quotas. Also use trace-based prefetch: watch for patterns where certain prompts appear X times in Y window then preseed those.

[10:52] Michael: what telemetry should we send to you to help tune?

[10:55] Samir: the most useful things are: per-request token counts, inter-arrival times, per-route latency histograms, kv hit/miss by endpoint, and GPU memory trends. Daniel you mentioned you have RPS traces?

[11:06] Daniel: yes I can upload the last 90 days. but it's large.

[11:10] Lena: even a week of p95 spikes is useful. we can downsample. we'll provide a small collector script you can run locally that strips PII and sends the necessary aggregates.

[11:24] Aisha: we have strict compliance; any data you need must be aggregated or we must run bench locally.

[11:29] Samir: understood — pilot options: 1) we run remote consult with aggregated telemetry, 2) we ship a bench harness to you and you run it on-prem (air-gapped), or 3) hybrid where we run bench on mirrored non-PHI subset in Redwood staging. Which do you prefer?

[11:45] Michael: option 2 sounds safest. we'll run the bench on-prem.

[11:49] Lena: great — we'll provide the harness, kv-warmup helper, and scheduler knobs in sample helm values. The bench harness includes experiments for varying max_num_seqs, latency_window_ms, slot sizes and quantization toggles.

[12:06] Daniel: any fast rules of thumb numbers for slot sizing? we currently have slot_size 128 tokens by default.

[12:12] Lena: slot_size is workload dependent. For short chat (median 80 tokens) a slot size of 96-128 is fine. But with many long-turn conversations, increase to 256 or use dynamic slot slicing. The runtime supports variable slot sizes per-priority.

[12:29] Aisha: what about multi-GPU model sharding for long contexts — do you recommend tensor parallel > pipeline for our workloads?

[12:36] Lena: for inference, pipeline parallelism can increase latency. We prefer model sharding strategies that keep KV locality — often data parallel with model sharding for very large models. There's a cost/law tradeoff: pipeline helps throughput but increases per-token latency.

[12:56] Michael: we have a couple security questions — SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration for Dedicated.

[13:03] Samir: Dedicated supports SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs shipped to your SIEM; keys can be integrated with your HSM/KMS. We'll include security whitepaper.

[13:12] Daniel: about rollout: after we run bench, what does success look like?

[13:16] Samir: success criteria: p95 < 400ms and p99 < 800ms under your target steady-state load with less than 15% cost increase from current baseline, and kv hit-rate > 90% for top templates. If we hit that, we'll convert bench into a 30-day pilot on Dedicated.

[13:33] Aisha: can we do canary routing during pilot?

[13:36] Lena: yes — Redwood Console supports canary splits and automatic rollback if latency or error budgets are exceeded.

[13:44] Michael: any gotchas with older 3090 nodes?

[13:47] Lena: older GPUs have lower throughput and different kernel performance — they can become stragglers. Use per-node capacity weights and prefer sending non-critical batchable traffic there. Also avoid using them for quant-critical low-latency routes.

[13:59] Samir: quick ping on competitor notes — you mentioned in-house runtime. we can help validate our runtime by sending benchmark harness that mirrors your in-house tests so you can compare apples-to-apples.

[14:09] Aisha: that would be useful. also can you include a small eval harness for quality checks when we toggle int4?

[14:14] Lena: yes, evaluation harness will run the 50 prompts you send and report ROUGE/BLEU/semantic similarity and some human-in-the-loop checks.

[14:24] Michael: okay let's recap next steps.

[14:27] Samir: recap — Samir to send pricing and SOW draft; Lena to send bench harness, kv-warmup helper script, scheduler knob examples and helm values; Daniel to share RPS trace and infra config; Aisha to provide 50 prompts. Customer will run bench on-prem and we'll reconvene after initial results.

[14:48] Daniel: timeline we hit — we'll aim to run bench the week of 2026-06-01.

[14:52] Samir: great. I'll follow up with calendar invites and secure link to bench artifacts. Thanks all — any final Qs?

[14:58] Michael: no, thanks for practical advice.

[15:01] Aisha: thanks all.

[15:03] Lena: thanks, bye.

[15:05] (call ends)
